definition: Insularity means narrow-mindedness caused by isolation from outside ideas.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word insularity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know insularity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The restaurant guide accused the city's chefs of insularity: no one had eaten anywhere but each other's dining rooms in years, and the menus showed it.
Wariness toward outsiders is just caution, and it can be dropped in a moment; insularity has hardened into a way of thinking.
Cliquishness closes one small circle at lunch tables and group chats; insularity goes further, sealing a whole community's thinking against the outside.

Parochialism is the parish's narrowness — judging every question by local terms and local interests. Insularity is the condition that produces such narrowness anywhere: a group sealed off from outside ideas until its thinking closes. A parochial board weighs only local concerns; insularity explains why no other concerns arrive.

Narrow-mindedness is closed thinking from any cause at all — stubbornness, vanity, fear, or plain habit. Insularity names one specific cause: isolation, the sealed loop that keeps outside ideas from ever arriving. Narrow-mindedness describes the closed mind itself; insularity blames the sealed environment around it.

Provincialism is the narrowness of the provinces — tastes and judgments formed far from the capital, unaware of the wider world. Insularity needs no map: it can seal a famous kitchen, a firm, or a capital city itself, wherever a group stops looking outward.

Insularity is the analyst's word - reviews, histories, and reports use it to explain why a group stopped taking in new ideas.

For most of a century, the Aldermann Orchestra filled its chairs from a single source: its own academy, whose teachers were themselves Aldermann players.
The sound that resulted was seamless — and sealed.
Players learned one bowing style, one tempo tradition, one list of approved composers, and passed them on unquestioned.
Musicians who trained elsewhere rarely auditioned; those who did described the process as a formality with a foregone ending.

A visiting critic, invited for the centenary, praised the ensemble's polish and then named its price: insularity, a loop so closed that no idea born outside the academy's walls had reached the stage in decades.
The board bristled, then quietly commissioned its first outside audit of auditions in ninety years.
